column2: Filled with anger, striking hand against hand, he said this to the king in a voice choked with tears:

My father was slain by base men through a most cruel deed, but I am not so tormented by that as by what has been done to you today, O king.
mahabharata:9:64.34	Hear this word of mine, lord, spoken in truth, by my sacrifices and charity, by dharma and by good deeds:
mahabharata:9:64.35	today, in the sight of Vasudeva, I shall send all the Panchalas by every means to the abode of the king of the dead. You ought to give me leave, great king.
Hearing the words of Drona's son, which brought joy to his mind, the Kaurava said to Kripa, "Teacher, quickly bring a pitcher filled with water."
Understanding the king's word, the best of Brahmanas took a full pitcher and came to the king's side.
Your son, great king, lord of men, said to him: "By my command, best of the twice-born, let Drona's son be consecrated as general. Good fortune to you, if you wish to please me.
A Brahmana, especially, must fight at the king's command, acting according to the kshatriya's dharma; so those who know dharma know."
Hearing the king's word, Kripa Sharadvata then consecrated Drona's son as general by the king's command.
Consecrated, great king, he embraced the best of kings and set out, making all the quarters resound with a lion's roar.
Duryodhana too, O king of kings, drenched in streams of blood, passed that night, terrifying to all beings.
Moving quickly away from that battlefield, O king, their minds agitated by grief, they gave themselves to thought and reflection.

Adopting a way of life like the moth's to the flame, which destroys oneself, one who fights fairly will surely lose his life; but by stratagem there may be success and great destruction of the enemy.

mahabharata:10:1.50	On this matter two verses are heard, sung of old by those who ponder dharma, seeing justice and seeing the truth of things:
mahabharata:10:1.51	The enemy's force should be struck when it is weary, when it is broken, when it is eating, when it is leaving and when it is entering,
mahabharata:10:1.52	when oppressed by sleep at midnight, when its leader is lost, when its warriors are divided, and when it is of two minds.
Thus Drona's son, the mighty, resolved on slaying the Pandavas and Panchalas as they slept in the battle.
Taking up that cruel purpose and deciding again and again, he woke the two sleeping ones, his uncle Kripa and the Bhoja Kritavarman.
They found no fitting reply there, being filled with shame; and he, after thinking a moment, said in a voice choked with tears:

King Duryodhana, the sole hero of great strength, for whose sake we became entangled in enmity with the Pandavas, is slain.

mahabharata:10:1.58	A most cruel deed was done by the petty Vrikodara, crushing with his foot the head of a consecrated king.

mahabharata:10:1.61	The neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants, and this very great lion-roar of heroes are heard.
mahabharata:10:1.62	From the eastern quarter, from the glad ones roaring loud, the hair-raising rumble of chariot wheels is heard.
mahabharata:10:1.63	In this slaughter of the Dhritarashtras by the Pandavas, only we three remain from that great massacre.
mahabharata:10:1.64	Some had the strength of a hundred elephants, some knew all weapons; they have been slain by the Pandavas—I think it is the turn of Time.
mahabharata:10:1.65	So it must truly have been fated, since such is the end of this undertaking though hard to do.
mahabharata:10:1.66	If your wisdom is not clouded by confusion, tell us what is best for us in this great calamity.
[Kripa said:] "All men are bound to two kinds of action; of fate and of human effort, there is nothing higher than these two.
Deeds do not succeed by fate alone, good one, nor by effort alone; success comes by the union of the two.
On these two all aims, high and low, depend, and men are seen engaged in them and likewise withdrawn.
What fruit does the rain bring, raining on a mountain? What fruit does it bring, not raining on a ploughed field?
The effort of one without fate, and fate for one without effort, is everywhere in vain; so what is the first principle there?
When the god has rained well and the field is well ploughed, the seed becomes of great quality; so human success comes about.
The wise decide that fate acts of its own accord, but the wise, relying on skill, strive in human effort.
By these two all the aims of men, bull among men, are accomplished; and men are seen striving and likewise withdrawn.
Deeds done are mostly seen to be fruitless on earth, while a deed not done is seen as giving grief; but not as of great fruit.
Whether one who makes no effort gains something by chance, or one who makes effort gains nothing, both are in a sad plight.
The skilled man can live; the lazy do not prosper in comfort; in this world of the living the skilled are mostly seen as well-wishers.
If a skilled man does not gain the fruit of his works after undertaking them, nothing can be said against him, and he still reaches the truth.
But one who stays idle in the world, gaining fruit without doing a deed, becomes an object of censure and is mostly hated.
One who acts otherwise than this, disregarding this, brings harm to himself; this is not the way of the wise.
When deprived of human effort, or again of fate, by either of these two causes, exertion may be fruitless; and a deed lacking human effort does not succeed here.
But one who, saluting the gods, rightly pursues his aims, skilled and with courtesy, is not baffled in vain.
And this is right striving: serving the elders, asking what is best, and acting on their beneficial words.
Rising again and again, one should ever consult those esteemed by the elders; they are the chief root of one's success, and success is said to rest on that root.
One who, having heard the words of the elders, applies himself to effort, soon obtains the fruit of effort rightly.
A man who pursues aims from passion, anger, fear or greed, who is powerless and scornful, soon falls from fortune.
This undertaking was begun by Duryodhana, greedy and short-sighted, without ability, from folly, without thought.
Disregarding those of good counsel and consulting with the wicked, though restrained, he made enmity with the more virtuous Pandavas.
Even before, being very ill-behaved, he does not deserve pity; when an aim fails he is tormented by not having done his friends' bidding.
Since we followed that sinful man, this dreadful great calamity has come to us also.
I too am tormented even today by this misfortune; thinking, my mind does not understand what is best for me.
A bewildered man should consult wise friends; and as they, consulted, advise, so should it be done.
So let us go together to Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and the greatly wise Vidura and ask them.
Asked, let them tell us what is best at once; and what they say we must do—this is my settled opinion.
Without undertaking deeds no aim is ever achieved; and those whose deeds, even with effort made, do not succeed, are struck by fate—there is no need for doubt here."
[Sanjaya said:] Burning with grief as with a blazing fire, hardening his mind, he replied to the two:

In each man there is his own judgment, and it seems fair to him; all are pleased, each with his own wisdom.

mahabharata:10:3.5	Everyone's own wisdom is established in his approval of it; they condemn another's judgment and repeatedly praise their own.

mahabharata:10:3.15	Every man, Bhoja, resolved that this is good," begins gladly to do it, even in deeds ending in death.
All men, knowing their own reasoning and wisdom, perform various efforts, knowing "this is beneficial."
The thought that has arisen in me today, born of calamity, I shall tell you both, a thought that destroys my grief.
The Prajapati, having created beings and ordained duty for them, placed in each class one quality as the best.
In the Brahmana, calm self-control; in the Kshatriya, the highest splendour; in the Vaishya and Shudra, skill and compliance with all classes.
An uncontrolled Brahmana is bad; a kshatriya without splendour is the lowest; an unskilled Vaishya is censured, and a refractory Shudra.
I was born in an excellent family, much honoured by Brahmanas, and by ill luck I have followed this kshatriya dharma.
Knowing the kshatriya's dharma, if I did a great deed in the way of a Brahmana, it would not be approved by good men.
Having borne knowledge of the bow and divine weapons in battle, having seen my father slain, what shall I say in the assembly?
So today, as I please, following the kshatriya's dharma, I shall go the road of the king and of my father of great splendour.
Today the Panchalas will sleep trustingly, victorious, with yokes and armour laid aside, filled with joy, thinking us conquered and dead, weary with this exertion.
As they sleep at night, at ease in their own camp, I shall make the night attack on the camp, hard to do.
Attacking them in the camp, like the dead, senseless, I shall slay them valiantly as Maghavan slew the Danavas.
Today I shall slay them all together, led by Dhrishtadyumna, valiantly, as a blazing fire a dry thicket; and having slain the Panchalas I shall find peace, good one.
I shall roam among the Panchalas, slaying them today in battle, like enraged Rudra himself, trident in hand, among beasts.
Today, having slain the Panchalas and cut them down, I shall afflict enraged in battle the sons of Pandu too.
Today, making the ground embodied with all the Panchalas, striking each one, I shall be quit of my debt to my father.
For Duryodhana, Karna, Bhishma and Saindhava, today I shall send the Panchalas on the road hard to travel.
Today in the night, when the night is gone, I shall crush by force the head of the Panchala king Dhrishtadyumna, like a beast's.
Today, Gautama (Kripa), I shall crush with a sharp sword in the night the sleeping sons of the Panchalas and Pandavas.
Today, having slain that Panchala army in the night, in the Sauptika, I shall be one whose task is done and happy, greatly wise one."
[Kripa said:] "We two shall follow you together at dawn; rest tonight, with armour and banner laid aside.
I shall follow you, and Kritavarman the Satvata, mounting our chariots and armoured, as you go against the enemy.
Together with us, best of chariot-warriors, you will slay the enemy tomorrow in the encounter, valiantly, the Panchalas with their followers.
You are able to show valour; rest tonight; you have long been awake, dear one; sleep this night.
Rested, awake from sleep, with a composed mind, giver of honour, meeting the enemies in battle you will surely slay them.
No one can conquer you, best of chariot-warriors, with weapons raised, not even among the gods, son of Fire.
Who could fight Drona's son in battle, enraged, going with Kripa and joined to Kritavarman, even the king of the gods?
We, well rested, awake, free of fever, will slay the enemies when the night has dawned.
Going to their camp and proclaiming your name in the battle, you will make great slaughter of the enemies who fight.
Having made slaughter of them on a clear dawn, sport as Shakra did after slaying the great asuras.
For you are able to conquer in battle the army of the Panchalas, as the enraged slayer of all the Danavas conquered the Daitya host.
With me with you in battle, guarded by Kritavarman, the lord himself, even the thunderbolt-bearer, could not withstand you.
Neither I nor Kritavarman, dear one, will ever withdraw from the battle without conquering the Pandavas.
Having slain the petty Panchalas with the Pandavas in the battle, we shall return, or we shall all be slain and go to heaven.
By every means we are your helpers at dawn; this I say truly to you, mighty-armed, blameless one."
Thus addressed by his uncle with beneficial words, Drona's son, rolling his eyes in anger, said to his uncle, O king:

How can one who is afflicted and intolerant sleep, one who thinks of his aims, or who is full of desire?

mahabharata:10:4.29	And this side of my friends, conquered while I live, increases my grief as a flood of water an ocean; for me, one-pointed today, where is sleep, where is comfort?
mahabharata:10:4.30	I consider them, guarded by Vasudeva and Arjuna, unassailable even by Mahendra, uncle.
mahabharata:10:4.31	I cannot in any way be restrained from this deed; I see none in this world who could turn me from it; this is my settled and virtuous decision.

[Kripa said:] "Likewise a clever man who does not learn humility, and who knows nothing, is also ignorant of the settled truth of dharma and wealth.
But a clever man who is obedient and has controlled senses can learn all the scriptures and does not oppose what is to be accepted.
But a man who is unrestrained and scornful, wicked and sinful, abandoning what is auspicious and fated, does much evil.
Friends hold back a man who has a protector from sin; the fortunate turns back, but the unfortunate does not turn back.
As a man of distracted mind is restrained by various words, so can he be restrained by a friend; but he who is not restrainable sinks.
Likewise the wise prevent a wise friend who is doing a sinful deed, again and again as best they can.
Set your mind on what is good, restrain yourself by yourself, and do my word, dear one, so that you will not grieve afterward.
The slaying of the sleeping is not honoured in the world by dharma, nor of those who have laid down their weapons, or whose chariots and horses are unyoked.
One who, being dishonest, would do harm to such persons in that condition would plainly sink in a vast, deep, boatless hell.
You are renowned in the world as the best among those who know all weapons, and never in this world was there in you the least fault.
And tomorrow, at sunrise, shining like the sun, you will conquer your foes in battle in the sight of all beings.
This deed, which is blameworthy, is unthinkable in you; to me it would be like a red stain placed on a white cloth."
[Ashvatthaman said:] "It is so as you say, uncle, I accept your counsel; but that bridge was first shattered into a hundred pieces by them.
In the sight of the kings and in your presence, my father, who had laid down his weapons, was felled by Dhrishtadyumna.
And Karna, best of chariot-warriors, whose chariot-wheel had sunk, in the utmost calamity, was slain by the wielder of Gandiva.
And Bhishma son of Shantanu, having laid down his weapons, weaponless, was slain by the wielder of Gandiva, putting Shikhandin in front.
The great archer Bhurishravas, sitting fasting in the battle, was felled by Yuyudhana while the kings cried out.
And Duryodhana, meeting Bhima in a mace-fight, was felled unrighteously in the sight of the kings.
That tiger among men, alone, surrounded by many great chariot-warriors, was felled unrighteously by Bhimasena.
The lament of the king with broken thighs, which I heard, told by the news-bearers, cuts my vitals.
Thus unrighteous and sinful are the Panchalas, breakers of the bridge; why do you not condemn those who have broken all bounds?
Having slain in the Sauptika night the Panchalas, slayers of my father, I would gladly be born a worm or a moth.
I am in haste today for what I wish to do; for me in haste, where is sleep, where is comfort?
No man has been born in the world, nor will be, who could turn me from this resolve made for their slaying."
[Sanjaya said:] Having said this, great king, mighty Drona's son yoked his horses in a secluded place and set out against the enemy.
The two great souls, Bhoja and Sharadvata, said to him: "Why is the chariot yoked, and what do you intend to do?
We two have set out in your company, bull among men; sharing grief and joy alike, you ought not to doubt us."
But Ashvatthaman, enraged, remembering his father's slaying, told them truly what he intended.

Having slain hundreds of thousands of warriors with sharp arrows, my father, with weapons laid down, was felled by Dhrishtadyumna.
mahabharata:10:5.33	Today I shall slay him in the same way, armour laid aside, that son of the Panchala king, sinner, by a sinful deed.
mahabharata:10:5.34	And how, having been slain by me like a beast, the sinful Panchala may gain the worlds won by weapon-fighting—so I think.

Having said this, he mounted his chariot and set out against the enemy, and Kripa followed him, O king, and Kritavarman the Satvata.
As they set out, those three, facing the enemy, shone like kindled sacrificial fires being invoked at a sacrifice.
They went to the enemy's camp, lord, where the people lay fast asleep, and reaching the gate Drona's son stood on his excellent chariot.
[Sanjaya said:] Having taken leave of Kritavarman and the great chariot-warrior Kripa, Drona's son, filled with anger, reached the camp gate.
There he saw a huge being of hair-raising aspect, of splendour like the moon and sun, standing blocking the gate.
Clad in a tiger skin dripping with blood, with a black antelope skin as upper garment, with a serpent as sacred thread,
with long, plump arms raised with many weapons, great serpents as armlets, his face wreathed in garlands of flame,
his mouth fearful with tusks, gaping, terrifying, adorned with thousands of wondrous eyes.
His body and his dress could not be described; seeing it in every way, even mountains would burst.
From his mouth, nostrils and ears everywhere, and from those thousands of eyes, great flames appeared.
From the rays of that splendour appeared hundreds and thousands of Hrishikeshas bearing conch, discus and mace.
That chariot-spear, striking him with its blazing tip, shattered, like a great meteor falling from the sky striking the sun at the end of an age.
Then he swiftly drew from its sheath a divine sword with a golden hilt, bright as the sky, like a blazing serpent from its hole.
Then the wise one hurled that excellent sword at the being, which on reaching the being vanished like cotton.
Then the enraged Drona's son hurled at it a blazing mace like Indra's standard, and the being swallowed that too.
Then, with no weapons left, looking here and there, he saw the sky made starless, filled with Janardanas.
Mortals do not go to heaven by sacrifices with fees, nor by austerities, nor by learning, as heroes slain in battle do.
I shall tell you this secret of the gods, O king; hear it, great king, as it happened of old.
As the wind drives clouds hither and thither, so, like a cloud, am I subject to the will of Time, the serpent's death.
By sacrifices alone the great-souled gods became superior; then the gods, active in rites, overcame the Danavas.
And any man who did any unpleasant thing to the son of Ambika became an object of hatred to the wise son of Kunti.
What Gandhari, afflicted with grief for her sons, her kin slain, said in distress, that has now come to pass.
Seeing her fallen, mighty Bhimasena, looking at Yajnaseni, said to the king of dharma:
The righteous king went on through that foul, inauspicious, hair-raising stench of corpses, pondering much.
